classification.reason: These words connect actions and things to location (in, inside) or direction of movement (into).

similarities: All three are connected to the idea of being in a space.
All three are common in daily conversation.
All three can appear with places like room, bag, box, and house.
differences: Use 'in' for position: The book is in my bag.
Use 'inside' for position with stronger focus on the inner part: Wait inside the car.
Use 'into' for movement from outside to inside: She walked into the classroom.
Choose 'in' for the normal, most neutral answer.
Choose 'inside' when you want to contrast with outside.
Choose 'into' after movement verbs like go, come, run, walk, put, jump.

association.note: Think in pairs: in/outside (position) and into/out of (movement).

counterExample.reason: This sounds unnatural for movement into a room. Use 'into' for direction: 'She went into the room.'

counterExample.wrong: My shoes are into the box.
counterExample.reason: No movement is happening now. This is position, so use 'in': 'My shoes are in the box.'
Do not use both here. Say 'Come in.' or 'Come inside.'

scenario.description: Office: Please put the files into the drawer, then keep them in order inside the folder. School: Students walk into the classroom and sit in their seats. Travel: We went into the museum because it was raining outside, then stayed inside for two hours. Daily conversation: Your phone is in your jacket pocket. Academic writing: The samples were placed in a glass container. Business email: Please upload the report into the shared drive folder by 5 p.m.

mnemonic.content: If there is no movement, use in or inside. If there is movement from outside to inside, use into.

confusion.confusedWith: in vs into; in vs inside
confusion.reason: Use 'into' for direction and movement, but 'in' for location. Use 'inside' when you want extra focus on the inner side or want to contrast with outside.
